whyChoose.title: Why Injured Holtville Residents Reach Out to Us

items.title: You Have Time, But Not Forever
items.desc: California law generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file a claim, though claims against a government agency can require notice in as little as six months. Acting sooner helps preserve evidence while it's still fresh.

items.title: Partial Fault Won't Shut You Out
items.desc: California follows a pure comparative fault rule, meaning even if you were partly responsible for what happened, you may still recover compensation reduced by your share of fault.

items.title: No Ceiling on Pain and Suffering Claims
items.desc: In ordinary injury cases, California places no cap on non-economic damages like pain, suffering, or loss of enjoyment of life.

items.title: You Pay Nothing Upfront
items.desc: Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so there's no fee unless they win or settle your case. That means the financial risk of getting help is on them, not you.

items.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Holtville?
items.answer: Under California law, you generally have two years from the date of the injury to file a claim. If your injury involves a government entity, such as a city vehicle or road hazard, the notice deadline can be as short as six months, so it's wise not to wait.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.answer: California uses a pure comparative fault system, which means you can still recover compensation even if you share some blame for what happened. Your recovery would simply be reduced by your percentage of fault, not eliminated.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to cluster in Holtville?
items.answer: Public collision records show that reported crashes in Holtville tend to peak on Saturdays between 6 and 8 p.m., with notable collision counts along 5th Street, Holt Avenue, Maple Avenue, and Walnut Avenue. These are neutral, record-based observations, not a statement about any particular road being unsafe.

items.question: Will I owe money if I contact LawProactive?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service that connects you with an independent attorney, and we are not a law firm ourselves. Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so they only get paid if you receive a settlement or award.

items.question: Is there a limit on how much I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: In most ordinary personal injury cases in California, there's no cap on non-economic damages such as pain and suffering. The specific value of any claim depends on the facts of your case, which an attorney can help evaluate.
